learningObjectives: Identify suitable use cases for cascading approvals versus a single approval
Compare the advantages of approvals using a reporting structure versus an authority matrix
Configure cascading approvals with an organizational hierarchy and with an authority matrix
Build conditional approval levels within a reporting hierarchy

elements.description: Approvals routed SEQUENTIALLY — one approver at a time. The next approver is asked only AFTER the current one approves. Not a parallel vote or majority tally — each level must approve in turn.

elements.text: Cascading approvals are like a chain of waterfalls: the case flows from one level of authority to the next, each approver reviewing and passing it downstream. Configure the chain with an authority matrix that maps reporting relationships — like water that must pass through every fall in sequence before reaching the pool at the bottom, with no fall skippable.

elements.description: A SINGLE approval has exactly one approver. A CASCADING approval chains multiple approvals together. Configure the Approval Step to cascade when work needs sign-off from a management chain or from several authorities before it can proceed.

elements.term: Two models for the approver chain
elements.description: REPORTING STRUCTURE — climbs the org chart from submitter upward (manager, manager's manager, etc.). AUTHORITY MATRIX — a decision table lists the specific approvers and conditions, including people OUTSIDE the reporting line.

Answer before configuring: (1) Who approves? (2) How many approvals? (3) Is the entire reporting hierarchy required or only a subset? (4) Are approvers outside the hierarchy needed? Answers 3–4 determine reporting structure vs. authority matrix.

A REJECTION at any level stops the cascade immediately — remaining approvers are never asked, and the Case routes to the configured rejection/rework path. Every approver in the chain must approve for the Case to pass.

elements.caption: Reporting structure climbs the manager hierarchy in order (how far up is conditional). Authority matrix uses a decision table — each satisfied condition adds an approver to an ordered list, including parties outside the reporting line.

elements.description: Configured in Dev Studio: add an Approve/Reject Step, select Cascading → Reporting structure. The approver comes from the operator's ID record (reporting or workgroup manager), and the cascade climbs the org chart automatically.

elements.term: Number of approvers: One / All / Custom
elements.description: Reporting structure offers three climb settings: ONE (immediate manager only), ALL (full hierarchy to the top), or CUSTOM (specific levels driven by When rules, e.g., small expenses stop at manager; large ones cascade further).

Select Cascading → Authority matrix in Dev Studio. The approver list is populated from a Decision Table, Data Page, Activity, or Data Transform. Each satisfied row adds its approver; Assignments route in list order.
CRITICAL: an authority matrix Decision table must be set to EVALUATE ALL ROWS — otherwise it stops at the FIRST matching row, returns only ONE approver, and the cascade is incomplete.

elements.term: When authority matrix beats reporting structure
elements.description: Use authority matrix when approvals must include people OUTSIDE the reporting structure — e.g., Legal, Compliance, Procurement. More flexible than reporting structure, which can only reach people in the management hierarchy.

examPitfalls.title: Cascading is SEQUENTIAL, not a parallel vote
examPitfalls.trapDescription: The biggest trap: thinking cascading approval is an 'any one / majority / 3-of-5' parallel tally. It is a chain — each approver is asked only after the prior one approves.
examPitfalls.bestPractice: Cascading = sequential levels; every approver in the determined chain must approve in turn.

examPitfalls.title: Single vs. cascading
examPitfalls.trapDescription: A question asks when cascading approval should be used instead of single approval. Candidates choose based on the number of approvers. Cascading approval is appropriate when the approval chain must follow the organizational hierarchy — single approval is for a fixed named approver regardless of org structure.
examPitfalls.bestPractice: Use cascading approval when sign-off must follow the organizational reporting hierarchy; use single approval when a specific named approver is always correct regardless of org structure.

examPitfalls.title: Reporting structure needs reports-to set
examPitfalls.trapDescription: Questions describe cascading approval failing to route correctly. Candidates blame the flow configuration. Cascading approval relies on the reports-to field in operator records — if it is not set, the chain cannot be resolved and routing fails.
examPitfalls.bestPractice: Org-hierarchy sign-off → reporting structure; ensure the manager chain is defined.

examPitfalls.title: Conditional levels live in reporting structure
examPitfalls.trapDescription: Varying HOW MANY levels based on Case data (e.g., amount) up the manager chain is a REPORTING-STRUCTURE feature (business logic / When), NOT the authority matrix.
examPitfalls.bestPractice: Same manager chain, depth varies by data → reporting structure with conditional levels.

examPitfalls.title: Authority matrix = decision table + outside-the-hierarchy parties
examPitfalls.trapDescription: Authority matrix is a decision table whose satisfied rows each add an approver (routed in list order). Its real differentiator is reaching approvers OUTSIDE the reporting line (Legal, Compliance, external).
examPitfalls.bestPractice: Approvers outside the manager chain, or condition-driven parties → authority matrix.

examPitfalls.title: Rejection stops the chain
examPitfalls.trapDescription: A rejection at any level halts the cascade — higher levels are never asked — and routes to the rejection/rework path.
examPitfalls.bestPractice: Configure the reject path; remaining approvers are not consulted after a rejection.

examPitfalls.title: Authority matrix decision table → 'Evaluate all rows'
examPitfalls.trapDescription: A decision table feeding an authority matrix must EVALUATE ALL ROWS to return the full list of approvers. By default it returns only the FIRST matching result, so only one approver is added.
examPitfalls.bestPractice: Set the decision table to 'Evaluate all rows' so every matching condition adds its approver.

examPitfalls.title: Reporting structure: One / All / Custom + approver source
examPitfalls.trapDescription: Reporting structure's number-of-approvers setting is One, All, or Custom (Custom uses When rules). The approver comes from the operator's Reporting Manager OR Workgroup Manager.
examPitfalls.bestPractice: Conditional depth → Custom (When rules). Approver = Reporting Manager or Workgroup Manager from the operator ID record.

examPitfalls.title: Authority matrix can be populated four ways
examPitfalls.trapDescription: The authority-matrix approver list can come from a Decision table, Data Page, Activity, or Data Transform — not only a decision table.
examPitfalls.bestPractice: Remember the four population sources; decision table is the most common.

practiceQuiz.scenario: A purchase request must be signed off by the submitter's manager, then that manager's manager, before it can proceed — each only after the previous one approves. Which approval configuration models this?

options.text: A cascading approval using a reporting structure — it climbs the manager chain sequentially, one level after another
A cascading approval with an 'any one approves' parallel threshold — the first manager to respond resolves it
A single approval Step routed to the top manager only
Two unrelated Case Types, one per manager

practiceQuiz.hint: Sequential sign-off up the manager chain = reporting-structure cascade.
practiceQuiz.rationale: A reporting-structure cascading approval routes to the manager, then the next manager up, sequentially B is wrong because cascading approval is not a parallel 'any one' vote — approvals happen in sequence..

practiceQuiz.scenario: An SA configures a reporting-structure cascading approval, but at runtime it fails to find any approver. What is the most likely cause?

options.text: The operators' manager / reports-to relationships are not configured, so Pega cannot climb the hierarchy
The Case has no SLA, which is mandatory for cascading approvals
Cascading approvals require a separate work queue per level, which was not created
The approval threshold was left at 'majority' instead of 'any one'

practiceQuiz.hint: Reporting structure walks the org chart — what must exist for that to work?
practiceQuiz.rationale: Reporting-structure cascades follow operators' manager/reports-to relationships; if the org chart is not set, there is no chain to climb B is wrong because an SLA is optional, not required for an approval to find approvers..

practiceQuiz.scenario: An expense approval always climbs the manager chain, but the NUMBER of levels depends on the amount: small amounts need only the manager; larger amounts also need a senior manager and a director. Which approach implements this?

options.text: Reporting structure with conditional levels — business logic (a When condition/threshold) on the amount sets how far up the chain to cascade
An authority matrix — only a decision table can vary how many approvers are required
A single approval whose approver changes based on the amount
A parallel approval whose threshold equals the dollar amount

practiceQuiz.hint: Same manager chain, depth varies by data — which model owns conditional levels?
practiceQuiz.rationale: Reporting structure supports conditional levels: business logic on Case data decides how far up the manager chain the cascade climbs B is wrong because the approvers here are all in the manager chain, so reporting structure (not an.

practiceQuiz.scenario: A contract needs approval from the submitter's manager AND from Legal and Compliance — neither of whom is in the submitter's reporting line — and only when the contract is high-risk. Which model fits best?

options.text: An authority matrix — a decision table adds Legal and Compliance based on conditions and can include approvers outside the reporting structure
Reporting structure — climbing the manager chain will eventually reach Legal and Compliance
Reporting structure with conditional levels set to three
A single approval routed to a shared Legal/Compliance queue

practiceQuiz.hint: Approvers outside the manager chain + condition-driven = which model?
practiceQuiz.rationale: An authority matrix (decision table) can require approvers outside the reporting line, adding Legal and Compliance based on conditions B is wrong because the manager chain never reaches Legal/Compliance unless they are the submitter's managers..

practiceQuiz.scenario: In an authority-matrix cascading approval, how are the required approvers determined and ordered at runtime?

options.text: A decision table is evaluated; each satisfied row adds its approver to a list, and Assignments are routed to them in the order they appear in the list
All operators in the application receive the approval and the majority decides
The matrix picks one approver at random to keep load balanced
The matrix climbs the reporting structure and ignores its own rows

practiceQuiz.hint: Each matching condition adds a party; routing follows list order.
practiceQuiz.rationale: The authority matrix is a decision table: every satisfied row adds its party to the approver list, and approvals are routed in list order B is wrong because there is no application-wide majority vote..

practiceQuiz.scenario: A three-level cascade is in progress: the direct manager approved; the director just rejected. What happens to the VP, who is next in the chain?

options.text: The cascade stops immediately — the VP is never asked an Assignment, and the Case routes to the configured rejection/rework path
The VP still receives the approval and can override the director's rejection
The cascade automatically restarts from the direct manager
All three responses are tallied and the majority outcome wins

practiceQuiz.hint: In a sequential chain, what does a single rejection trigger for the cascade?
practiceQuiz.rationale: A rejection at any level ends the sequential cascade; higher levels are not asked and the Case follows the rejection path B is wrong because higher levels do not review or override a rejected request..

practiceQuiz.scenario: A BA claims: 'Cascading approval sends the request to all approvers at once and proceeds when most of them approve.' Why is this incorrect?

options.text: Cascading approvals are sequential — the next approver is asked only after the current one approves; there is no simultaneous send or majority tally
It is correct — cascading is Pega's parallel majority-vote feature
It is incorrect only because approvers are always work queues, never individuals
It is incorrect because cascading approvals never reject — they only approve

practiceQuiz.hint: Recall the defining sequential behavior of a cascading approval flow.
practiceQuiz.rationale: Cascading approval is a sequential chain: each level is asked in turn, and a rejection stops it — there is no parallel 'most of them approve' vote B is wrong because that parallel majority model is not how Pega cascading approvals work..

practiceQuiz.scenario: A BA is explaining approval routing models to a client manager choosing between reporting-structure and authority-matrix approaches. Which TWO statements correctly contrast the reporting-structure and authority-matrix approval models?

options.text: Reporting structure climbs the manager (reports-to) chain; the number of levels can be made conditional with business logic
Authority matrix is a decision table that can require approvers outside the reporting line, adding each based on a condition
Reporting structure can include approvers from any department regardless of the org chart
Authority matrix sends the request to everyone at once and resolves on a majority vote

practiceQuiz.hint: One climbs the org chart (conditionally); the other is a decision table reaching outside it.
practiceQuiz.rationale: Reporting structure climbs the manager chain with optional conditional levels, and the authority matrix is a decision table that can add approvers outside the hierarchy by condition C is wrong because reporting structure is limited to the manager chain — it cannot reach arbitrary departments..

practiceQuiz.scenario: An authority-matrix cascading approval is backed by a decision table, but at runtime only ONE approver is ever added even though several rows should match. What is the most likely fix?

options.text: Set the decision table to 'Evaluate all rows' so it returns the full list of approvers instead of stopping at the first match
Switch the approval from cascading to single, because authority matrices support only one approver
Add an SLA so the table re-evaluates and collects more approvers
Move the decision table into the reporting structure model

practiceQuiz.hint: A decision table returns one result by default — how do you make it return a list?
practiceQuiz.rationale: By default a decision table returns only the first matching row's result; setting 'Evaluate all rows' makes it return the full list of approvers the authority matrix needs.

practiceQuiz.scenario: For a reporting-structure cascade, an SA wants approvals to climb the ENTIRE management hierarchy to the top — no conditions. Which 'number of approvers' setting is correct, and where does the approver come from?

options.text: 'All' — the cascade climbs the full manager hierarchy; the approver is the operator's Reporting Manager or Workgroup Manager from the operator ID record
'Custom' — you must always write a When rule even to climb the whole hierarchy
'One' — selecting one approver automatically continues to the top
There is no such setting; you must list each manager by name

practiceQuiz.hint: One / All / Custom — which one means 'whole hierarchy'?
practiceQuiz.rationale: 'All' climbs the entire manager hierarchy, and the approver at each level is the operator's Reporting Manager or Workgroup Manager B is wrong because 'All' needs no When rule — Custom is only for a conditional number of.

practiceQuiz.scenario: Where and how do you configure a cascading approval (either model) according to the academy module?

options.text: In Dev Studio: add an Approve/Reject Step to the Case Life Cycle, select Cascading, then choose Reporting structure or Authority matrix
In App Studio only: cascading is a checkbox on the Case Type's data model
In Admin Studio: cascading approvals are a runtime system setting
In Prediction Studio: an adaptive model selects approvers automatically

practiceQuiz.hint: Approve/Reject Step + Cascading + model — in which studio?
practiceQuiz.rationale: The module configures cascading approvals in Dev Studio: add an Approve/Reject Step, select Cascading, then Reporting structure or Authority matrix. B is wrong because it is not a data-model checkbox. C is wrong because Admin Studio handles runtime administration, not approval design. D is wrong because Prediction Studio builds ML models, not approval chains.

practiceQuiz.scenario: A Pega application uses cascading approvals. The authority matrix is configured to resolve the approval chain based on the 'ReportingManager' relationship in the operator directory. After a front-line employee submits a request, the system must determine who the first approver is. Which data source does Pega consult to identify the first approver?

options.text: The operator directory (operator record of the submitting user), which contains the ReportingManager relationship used by the authority matrix
The Access Group of the submitting user, which lists approvers in order of seniority
The SLA rule attached to the case, which names the escalation targets who also serve as approvers
The Work Group configuration, which stores the approval chain for all members of that group

practiceQuiz.hint: What data source does the authority matrix query to find the first cascading approver?
practiceQuiz.rationale: The authority matrix traverses the ReportingManager relationship starting from the submitter, climbing the org chart until all required approvers have acted. The chain is dynamic — it adapts to each submitter's actual reporting structure.

practiceQuiz.scenario: An SA is deciding between Cascading Approval and a single-level Approval Step for a contract sign-off process. Which TWO statements correctly identify when Cascading Approval is the appropriate choice?

options.text: Cascading Approval is appropriate when multiple levels of authority must each independently review and approve the same request
Cascading Approval allows conditional levels so that not every Case requires the same number of approvers
Cascading Approval is the only option when two approvers must review simultaneously in parallel
Single-level Approval is always preferred because Cascading Approval cannot be configured in App Studio

practiceQuiz.hint: Cascading Approval is for sequential multi-level sign-offs, with optional conditional levels to skip tiers.
practiceQuiz.rationale: Cascading Approval is designed for sequential multi-level sign-offs where each approver acts one after another. Conditional approval levels allow tiers to be skipped based on Case data (e.g., loan amount). Cascading Approval is not for simultaneous parallel reviews, and it can be configured in App Studio.

practiceQuiz.scenario: An SA configures a Cascading Approval using a reporting hierarchy with up to three management levels. Which TWO behaviors correctly describe this configuration at runtime?

options.text: The approval routes first to the submitter's direct reporting manager, then escalates upward if the manager approves and the next level is required
Conditional approval levels can skip a management tier when a Case condition (such as contract value) is not met
All three management levels are notified simultaneously at the time the approval is submitted
A reporting-structure cascade always requires an authority matrix to define which approver handles each level

practiceQuiz.hint: Reporting-structure cascades are sequential from the direct manager upward, with conditions able to bypass levels.
practiceQuiz.rationale: In a reporting-structure cascade, the approval starts with the direct manager and escalates upward level by level. Conditional levels allow specific tiers to be bypassed when Case conditions (like contract value) are not met. All levels are not notified simultaneously, and an authority matrix is an alternative approach, not a requirement for reporting-structure cascades.

quickRecap.value: A SEQUENTIAL chain of approvers (one level at a time) — not a parallel any-one/majority vote.
One approver → single; multiple approvers in sequence → cascading.
Climbs the manager (reports-to) chain automatically; org chart must be configured.
Business logic on Case data (e.g., amount) sets HOW FAR up the reporting cascade goes.
Reporting structure: One (manager) / All (whole hierarchy) / Custom (When rules for conditional levels). Approver = Reporting or Workgroup Manager.
A decision table; each satisfied row adds an approver (routed in list order). Reaches parties OUTSIDE the reporting line (Legal, Compliance, external).
Approver list from a Decision table, Data Page, Activity, or Data Transform. Decision table must 'Evaluate all rows' to return the full list (else only the first result).
Manager chain → reporting structure; approvers outside the hierarchy / condition-driven parties → authority matrix.
A rejection at any level stops the chain; higher levels are not asked; routes to the rejection path.
Approve/Reject Step → Cascading → Reporting structure OR Authority matrix. First ask: who, how many, whole hierarchy or subset, anyone outside it?
